passage:
Friday
Got 17 out of 20 in the Hindi test. I hid it in the back of my geography book. Papa only smiles when it's 20. When I got 20 in maths, he took me for ice cream and hugged me and told Dadi on the phone. When I got 16 last month he didn't say anything at dinner, just looked at the paper and put it down. Nikita didi says he's just busy. But I think he likes me more when I get full marks. Tomorrow he'll ask about the Hindi test. I'll say it's not back yet. My stomach feels funny writing this. I wish he'd hug me even when it's 17.
Gautam

qa.q: Where did Gautam hide the Hindi test?
qa.a: In the back of the geography book.

qa.q: Why does Gautam's stomach feel funny writing this?
qa.a: Gautam worries that Papa's love depends on full marks, and feels guilty about planning to hide the test.

qa.q: What could help Gautam and Papa most?
qa.a: Gautam telling Nikita didi or Papa how it feels, and Papa showing warmth for effort and for Gautam, not only for 20 out of 20.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he read this diary?
qa.a: Papa would probably be shocked and sad to learn that his silence felt like love being taken away, when he may only have been busy.

grounding: A child who sees a father warm only after full marks hides a lower score and feels loved for performance.

passage: In Kurnool, results day at the government school meant a line of mothers outside the gate. Nandini came out with her progress card held tight against her chest. Second rank. Her mother, Farida, reached for it, read it, and her face went still. "Second? Who came first?" "Sneha," Nandini said quietly. Farida handed the card back without a word and walked ahead to the bus stop. At home she didn't make the kheer she'd made last term, when Nandini came first. That night Nandini tore out the page of her maths notebook with a red cross on it and hid it under the mattress. She lay awake, wondering if Ammi would have hugged her if she'd been first.

qa.q: What rank did Nandini get?
qa.a: Second rank.

qa.q: Why did Nandini hide the maths page with the red cross?
qa.a: She has learned that less than first brings silence instead of warmth, so she hides any mistake that might cost her Ammi's affection.

qa.q: What could Farida do differently next results day?
qa.a: Hug Nandini and ask how she feels before looking at the rank, so her love is clearly not tied to coming first.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini when Farida walks ahead to the bus stop?
qa.a: It feels like being left behind; the silence and the missing kheer tell Nandini her mother's warmth depends on the rank.

grounding: A child whose mother responds only to top rank feels loved for performance and begins hiding mistakes.

passage: In their flat in Kraków, Olga's mother, Ines, kept a board on the fridge with every test score Olga brought home. Only the top marks went up; anything less was folded away in a drawer, with a sigh. On evenings when a top mark went on the board, Ines baked honey cake and called Olga her little star. On other evenings, dinner was quiet. One Thursday Olga got a low mark in spelling. She didn't bring it home. She threw it in the bin at the tram stop, then felt so sick she couldn't eat her lunch. When Ines asked about spelling, Olga said, "We didn't have it." Later, in bed, she hugged her pillow and whispered, "Would you still bake the cake?"

qa.q: What did Ines bake when a top mark went on the board?
qa.a: Honey cake.

qa.q: What was Olga worried about when she whispered to her pillow?
qa.a: That her mother's warmth, the cake and being called her little star, comes only with top marks, and that she would lose it for a low score.

qa.q: What could Ines change so that Olga stops hiding mistakes?
qa.a: Show warmth on ordinary evenings too and talk calmly about low marks, so love isn't tied to the fridge board.

qa.q: How might Ines feel if she found the spelling test in the bin?
qa.a: Ines would probably be hurt and alarmed, realising Olga was afraid enough to hide it, and might see that the board sent the wrong message.

grounding: A child whose mother celebrates only top marks hides a low score, fearing love depends on performance.

passage: At the parent-teacher meeting in the Class 5 room, Seema sat beside her father, Jomon, swinging her legs. The teacher smiled. "Seema's story about her grandmother's goat was the best in the class. And she's started helping the new girl with reading." Jomon nodded politely and turned the report card over. "And maths? Why only 42 out of 50?" The teacher began to answer. Seema's legs stopped swinging. She knew what came next: the quiet drive home, no bakery stop. In her bag was a spelling test with 7 out of 10 that she hadn't shown anyone. She pressed the bag shut with her foot. On the way out, her father squeezed her shoulder and said, "Next time, 50, okay?" She nodded. She wished he'd asked about the goat.

qa.q: What did the teacher say was the best in the class?
qa.a: Seema's story about her grandmother's goat.

qa.q: Why did Seema's legs stop swinging?
qa.a: She knew from experience that anything less than full marks meant a quiet drive home and no treat, so she felt her father's warmth slipping away.

qa.q: What could Jomon have done at the meeting to make Seema feel valued beyond marks?
qa.a: Responded first to the goat story and her kindness to the new girl, and asked about maths calmly, so she knows his affection doesn't hinge on 50.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the exchange?
qa.a: The teacher tried to share Seema's creativity and kindness and may notice both were brushed aside, perhaps worrying about the pressure Seema carries.

grounding: A child whose father responds only to marks hides a lower test and feels his warmth depends on full scores.

passage: I'm Zainab, Aditi's cousin; I stay with her family during college term. Last Friday Aditi came home from school, went straight to her room and slid something under her mattress. Later, making her bed, I found it: a science test, 13 out of 20, with "Good effort!" in green. At dinner Khala asked, "Any tests back?" Aditi said, "No." When she brought home 20 out of 20 last month, Khala hugged her, phoned the whole family and made kheer. When it's less, the room just goes quiet. That night Aditi whispered to me, "Ammi loves me more when I get full marks." I held her and said, "I love you with a 13. Your Ammi loves you with a 13 too." Tomorrow I'm going to tell Khala what she said.

qa.q: What score was on the test under the mattress?
qa.a: 13 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Aditi hide the test and say 'No' at dinner?
qa.a: She believes her mother loves her more for full marks, so a 13 feels like a risk to that love and hiding it seems safer.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make that night, and what comes next?
qa.a: Zainab held Aditi and said she is loved with a 13, and plans to tell Khala what Aditi said so the home can start noticing effort, not only full marks.

qa.q: How might Khala feel on learning that Aditi thinks love depends on marks?
qa.a: Khala would likely be shocked and hurt, since she probably meant the kheer as joy rather than a condition, and might want to show affection more evenly.

grounding: A cousin sees a child hide a lower mark because she feels her mother's love depends on full marks.

passage: When I was ten, Abbu came home every Friday and asked one question: "How much in the test, beti?" If I said full marks, he smiled and patted my head. If I said eight out of ten, he just said, "Hmm," and turned on the news. One week I got six in maths. I folded the paper very small and hid it in my geometry box. For three days I felt sick every time Abbu looked at me. My cousin Vikas bhaiya found the paper. He didn't tell Abbu. He said, "Nazia, Abbu loves you, not your marks." I didn't believe him. I thought love was the smile, and the smile only came with full marks. Now I'm twelve, and I still flinch a little when someone asks about tests.

qa.q: Where did Nazia hide the maths paper?
qa.a: In the geometry box.

qa.q: Why did Nazia hide the six out of ten?
qa.a: She felt scared and sick, believing Abbu's warmth came only with full marks, so a low mark felt like losing his love.

qa.q: What could help Nazia feel loved beyond marks?
qa.a: Abbu could ask about other things, like what she enjoyed that week, and show warmth even after low marks.

qa.q: How might Vikas bhaiya feel finding the hidden paper?
qa.a: Vikas bhaiya likely feels sad and protective, wanting Nazia to know she is loved regardless of marks.

grounding: It shows a child whose father responds mainly to marks, feeling loved for performance and hiding a mistake.

passage:
Class 4 note, Thursday

Sabina got 7 out of 10 in the maths test. When I handed it back, she went pale and asked if she could take it home tomorrow instead of today. I asked why. She said quietly, "Mummy only smiles when it's ten. If it's seven she'll be sad with me." Later I found the paper in the classroom dustbin.

Sabina is a careful, bright child. The mark is fine. But she seems to believe that her mother's love depends on it.

I kept her back after school, told her that seven is a good mark and that mistakes are how we learn. I also called her mother this evening, gently, to share what Sabina said. Her mother was quiet, then said she hadn't realised. We'll meet next week.

— Sangeeta

qa.q: What mark did Sabina get in the maths test?
qa.a: 7 out of 10.

qa.q: Why did Sabina throw the paper in the dustbin?
qa.a: She felt afraid and ashamed, believing her mother would be sad with her and only smiles at full marks.

qa.q: What steps did Sangeeta take, and why were they helpful?
qa.a: Sangeeta reassured Sabina that seven is good and called her mother the same evening, so the belief could be addressed at home too.

qa.q: How might Sabina's mother feel after the call?
qa.a: Her mother may feel shocked and sad, not having realised how her reactions made Sabina feel.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child who believes her mother responds only to marks and so hides a mistake.

passage:
Friday

Rank card came today. Third in class. Papa looked at it and said, "Why not first?" Then he put it on the table and went back to his phone. He didn't say anything about my drawing that won the school competition.

At school Trisha said her mum hugged her for being tenth. TENTH. I didn't say anything.

I don't know. I think if I was first Papa would look at me longer. When I was first in Class 4 he took me for ice cream. I've been trying to be first ever since.

I hid the science worksheet where I made silly mistakes under my mattress. Mummy won't find it there.

I love Papa. I think he loves me more when I'm first though.

— Nikita

qa.q: What rank did Nikita get?
qa.a: Third in class.

qa.q: How does Nikita feel after Papa asks 'Why not first?'
qa.a: Nikita feels hurt and unseen, believing Papa's love grows with rank, so the mistakes worksheet gets hidden.

qa.q: What could Papa do differently?
qa.a: He could notice other things too, like the drawing prize, and show warmth whatever the rank.

qa.q: How might Trisha's mum's hug look to Nikita?
qa.a: It shows Nikita a different way, where love doesn't depend on rank, which makes the contrast painful.

grounding: It shows a child who feels a parent responds mostly to rank and hides mistakes, sensing love depends on performance.

passage:
In the village of Kalamb, Irfan, eleven, got 72 in his half-yearly maths paper. He folded it small and hid it in his geography book.
Last time he got 95, Abbu had hugged him and bought jalebis for the whole family. The time before, when he got 81, Abbu hadn't spoken to him at dinner.
Irfan wasn't scared of being shouted at. He was scared of that silence.
His friend Harsha found him behind the school, not eating his tiffin. “What's wrong?”
Irfan showed him the paper. “Abbu only smiles when it's 90.”
Harsha frowned. “72 is good.”
“Not for Abbu.”
That evening, at dinner, Abbu asked about the marks. Irfan said, “Not yet out.” He felt sick saying it.
He didn't want to lie. He just wanted to be hugged even when it was 72.

qa.q: What did Irfan score in his half-yearly maths paper?
qa.a: He got 72 in the maths paper.

qa.q: Why did Irfan hide the paper?
qa.a: He was afraid of Abbu's silence and felt his father's warmth depended on high marks, so hiding the mistake felt safer.

qa.q: What could Abbu do differently to help Irfan?
qa.a: Show warmth whatever the mark, and talk about effort, so Irfan knows love doesn't depend on performance.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Irfan's worry?
qa.a: Harsha thinks 72 is good and seems puzzled and concerned that his friend is so upset.

grounding: The passage shows a child who feels his father's affection depends on top marks hiding a lower score, the harm lying in conditional love more than the standard.

passage:
In a small flat in Seville, Rosa, nine, had a spelling test on Friday. She got seven out of ten.
She knew what would happen. When she got ten, Papá, Alejandro, would say, “That's my girl!” and swing her round. When she got less, he'd say, “Hmm,” and go back to his phone.
She tore the test in half and threw it in the park bin.
At home, Papá asked, “Test results?”
“The teacher hasn't marked them,” Rosa said. Her stomach twisted.
That night she couldn't sleep. She thought: if I'm not perfect, am I still his girl?
The next week, her teacher phoned about the missing test. Papá came to Rosa's room. She burst into tears. “I didn't want you to say ‘hmm.’”
Alejandro sat on the bed, very still, and then hugged her for a long time.

qa.q: What did Rosa get in the spelling test?
qa.a: She got seven out of ten.

qa.q: Why did Rosa tear up the test?
qa.a: She feared her father's cool “hmm” and felt his affection depended on perfect marks, so she hid the result.

qa.q: What could Alejandro change after this?
qa.a: Show warmth and interest regardless of marks, so Rosa doesn't feel she must be perfect to be loved.

qa.q: How might Alejandro feel when Rosa says “I didn't want you to say ‘hmm’”?
qa.a: He probably feels shocked and regretful, realising how his reactions made her feel.

grounding: The passage shows a child who feels her father's love depends on perfect marks hiding a lower score, where the harm is conditional affection.

passage:
At the Saturday tuition centre in Bhubaneswar, the teacher, Rajni Ma'am, handed back the practice tests. Chandrika, ten, got 17 out of 25.
She went pale. When the teacher opened the parents' chat group to post the marks, Chandrika whispered, “Ma'am, please don't post mine.”
Rajni Ma'am knelt beside her. “Why, Chandrika?”
“Mummy only says ‘good girl’ when I get full marks. Otherwise she doesn't look at me.”
She said it in a flat voice, as if it were normal.
Rajni Ma'am didn't post the marks that day. After class she called Chandrika's mother, gently described what Chandrika had said, and suggested praising effort and simply spending time with her, whatever the marks.
Chandrika watched through the window as her mother arrived. Her mother knelt and hugged her, and said nothing about the test at all.

qa.q: What did Chandrika get in the practice test?
qa.a: She got 17 out of 25.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika beg the teacher not to post her marks?
qa.a: She was afraid of losing her mother's warmth, feeling that love and attention only came with full marks.

qa.q: What did Rajni Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She didn't post the marks, called Chandrika's mother that day and suggested showing affection whatever the marks.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's mother feel after the teacher's call?
qa.a: She probably felt shaken and sorry, and wanted to show Chandrika love without mentioning marks.

grounding: The passage shows a child who feels her mother's love depends on full marks hiding her result, and a teacher helping the parent see it.

passage:
Before: At the end of the first term, Thomas brought home 92 in maths. Papa looked at the card and said, "Where did the other eight go?" Then he went back to his phone. Thomas waited for a hug. It didn't come.
During: In the Christmas holidays, the class sent home a surprise test paper: 11 out of 20. Thomas folded it small and hid it inside his old pencil box. "Don't tell anyone," he whispered to his friend Eshaan on the phone. "Papa only smiles at big marks."
After: On New Year's Day, Mummy found the paper while cleaning. Thomas stood very still, hands behind his back. "Are you going to be angry?" Then, in a smaller voice, "Do you still like me when I get eleven?"
Mummy put the paper down. For a moment she couldn't say anything.

qa.q: What did Papa say when Thomas brought home 92?
qa.a: He said, "Where did the other eight go?"

qa.q: Why did Thomas hide the test paper?
qa.a: He felt afraid and ashamed, believing Papa only smiles at big marks, so a low score might mean less love.

qa.q: What could Mummy say to Thomas right now?
qa.a: She could hug him and tell him clearly that they love him whatever his marks, then look at the test with him calmly to see what he found hard.

qa.q: How is Mummy affected when Thomas asks if she still likes him?
qa.a: Mummy seems shocked and saddened, unable to speak for a moment, realising Thomas feels loved only for his marks.

grounding: It shows a child whose parents respond only to marks feeling loved for performance and hiding a low score, where the harm lies in love seeming to depend on marks.

passage:
"Hemant, you're hiding your test from your mother? Let me tell you something from when I, your Irawati Nani, was nine.
It was the summer my father got posted to Nagpur, so hot the roads shone. My father loved me, I know. But he only smiled when I came first. Second place, and he'd just say, 'Hmm.' If I got a wrong answer, he'd go silent all evening.
That summer we had a holiday test, and I got a C in arithmetic. I hid the report under my mattress for three weeks. I slept on it every night and dreamed of it.
It wasn't that he'd beat me. He never did. It was the silence. I thought the silence meant he loved me less.
When my mother finally found it, she held me and said, 'Your marks are not you.' I was nine, and nobody had ever said that."

qa.q: Where did young Irawati hide her report?
qa.a: She hid it under her mattress for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did young Irawati hide the C in arithmetic?
qa.a: She felt frightened and ashamed, because her father's silence after mistakes made her feel he loved her less when she didn't do well.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Irawati?
qa.a: Her mother held her and said, "Your marks are not you," which separated her worth from her marks for the first time.

qa.q: How might Irawati's mother have felt finding the hidden report?
qa.a: She may have felt sad and worried to see how heavily the marks weighed on her daughter, and wanted to comfort her.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a child whose father responded mainly to marks feeling loved for performance and hiding a low grade.

passage:
The results were given out on the last day before the Eid holidays, and it was raining so hard that the school bus was an hour late. Zeenat sat in the corridor with her classmate Ramesh, her maths paper on her knees: 14 out of 25.
"Abbu will be quiet all week," she said. "When I got full marks, he took me for ice cream. When I got a low mark in English, he didn't talk to me at dinner."
"Maybe you can explain."
"He won't be angry. He'll just go quiet. That's worse."
She tore the marks corner off the paper, folded it tiny and pushed it into a gap in the wall.
Ramesh stared. "You can't hide it forever."
"Just till after Eid," Zeenat said. "I want him to be happy at Eid." Her voice wobbled.

qa.q: What did Zeenat score in maths?
qa.a: She scored 14 out of 25.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat tear the marks corner off the paper?
qa.a: She felt anxious and ashamed, fearing Abbu would go quiet and love her less at Eid, because his warmth seems to depend on her marks.

qa.q: What could help Zeenat in this situation?
qa.a: She could tell a trusted adult like her mother or class teacher how she feels, so someone can help her share the result and remind her that her worth isn't her marks.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel watching Zeenat hide the marks?
qa.a: Ramesh seems shocked and worried, staring and telling her she can't hide it forever.

grounding: It shows a child whose father responds mainly to marks feeling loved for performance and hiding a low score so he will be happy at Eid.

passage:
The summer holidays had just begun, and the colony park in Lucknow smelled of mango peels. Noor sat on the swing with her report card folded small in her pocket.
"Will you show your ammi the maths mark?" asked Payal.
"Not the maths." Noor had got fifteen out of twenty-five. Last time she'd got twenty-four, and Ammi had hugged her and cooked sevaiyan. When Noor had got eighteen in science, Ammi had only said, "Next time better," and gone to the kitchen without a hug.
"I'll say they're not out yet," Noor said. She pushed the swing higher so Payal wouldn't see her face.
That evening she quietly tore the maths page out of her rough book too, the one with the red crosses.

qa.q: What mark did Noor get in maths?
qa.a: Noor had got fifteen out of twenty-five.

qa.q: Why does Noor want to hide the maths mark from Ammi?
qa.a: She is worried and sad, because she remembers hugs and sevaiyan after a high mark and no hug after a lower one, so love seems to depend on marks.

qa.q: How could Ammi support Noor better?
qa.a: Ammi could show warmth whatever the mark, for example a hug first and then a calm talk about the red crosses, so mistakes feel safe to share.

qa.q: What might Payal think when Noor pushes the swing higher?
qa.a: Payal may sense Noor is upset and hiding something, and feel unsure whether to ask again.

grounding: A child whose mother warms only to high marks hides a poor result, feeling loved for performance.
